blurb: Racket sport where a feathered shuttlecock is hit over a high net, in singles or doubles.
Tennis and volleyball combined: played on sand with solid, stringless paddles.
Doubles racket sport on a small court enclosed by glass and mesh walls, where the ball may be played off the walls. Not pop tennis, which is an open court with a low net.
Paddle sport for two or four players: a perforated plastic ball over a low net on a small court.
Fast game with a hollow rubber ball in a walled court, played off every wall.
The original indoor racket game that modern tennis grew out of, played in a walled court with sloping roofs.
Two or four players hit a small rubber ball off the walls of a four-walled court.
Ping-pong: a light plastic ball is hit across a table net with small paddles.
Racket sport for singles or doubles: a felt-covered ball is hit over a net on hard, clay or grass courts.
American game of hitting a small rubber ball against a single wall with paddles; the ball may bounce on the floor only once between hits. Popular outdoors.
Paddleball in a court with a front wall and two side walls, often a handball court; players hit a rubber ball with a paddle.
Indoor paddle game played in a four-walled court; invented in 1930 at the University of Michigan. Run by the National Paddleball Association.
Racquetball variant played on a squash court with a larger-headed racquet and a bouncier ball than squash.
Indian racket sport played with a wool ball instead of a shuttlecock.
Pelota specialty played with tennis-type rackets and a rubber ball against the front wall of a 30 m fronton; only pairs play at world level. Born in Mexico around 1900.
Team Basque pelota played mostly in France: two teams of three with a long basket-glove on an open court 16 m wide and 100 m long, with no side walls.
Called cesta punta by the federation: players catch the ball in a curved wicker basket and hurl it at the front wall at up to 300 km/h. Spain and France lead.
Basque basket-glove game with a shorter, shallower glove than cesta punta; the ball may be held only briefly. The name means 'pure game'. Men only.
Basque pelota with a one-piece short wooden bat and a thick leather ball, played in pairs on a 36 m fronton. A very physical specialty; Spain leads.
Basque pelota with a wooden paleta and the smallest of the leather balls, on a 36 m fronton or a trinquet. Fast and spectacular; Spain, France and Argentina lead.
The most widely played Basque pelota specialty: a wooden, carbon or fibreglass paleta and a rubber ball on a 30 m fronton or trinquet. Born in South America.
Players throw, rather than hit, a very lively leather ball with a net-strung wicker ring, played in pairs on a trinquet. France dominates.
Rare English school game played with a wooden bat and a leather ball in a purpose-built court called the Ball Place, at Downside School in Somerset.
Brazilian beach racket game where two partners rally a ball back and forth.
Tennis variant played without a net: serves and rallies are aimed at the opponent's no-man's land, split into two halves. Invented in Italy in 2020.
Peruvian wall-and-ball sport rooted in Basque pelota.
Tennis-like street game from Barbados, played with wooden paddles.
Beach paddle game known in Israel as matkot: partners rally a small rubber ball with wooden paddles, trying to keep it in the air as long as possible.
Tennis-style game on a 44 x 20 ft court with a paddle and a low-pressure ball; underhand serve, first to four points wins a game. Created in 2016 in Northern California.
Italian court game, invented in the 16th century, played with a tambourine-style bat.
Paddle-and-ball game for two to four players, played on concrete, grass or sand.
Racket game on a round court around a central disc that players can move all the way around; singles or doubles.
Brazilian game played with a racket in each hand and a tennis ball over a net about 1.15 m high on a 14 x 4.5 m court.
Team racket game mixing volleyball, badminton and tennis: players hit a large light ball over a net, and it may bounce once between hits. Created in Michigan in the 1980s.
Small-court version of tennis, first recorded in 1984.
Paddle game on a tennis or pickleball court where the ball may bounce up to twice on a side; 2 to 6 players, paddles and 50 mm rubber balls or racquetballs.
Badminton-style game for two to four players, played with paddles and a birdie.
Tennis played with a glove-style racket worn on the hand instead of a strung racket, promoted as the original hand-hit form of tennis.
Brazilian net game based on peteca: players hit a feathered shuttle over a net with the hand or a racket.
Two-player paddle game played with a birdie or a ball.
Racket game where a rubber ball on a cord is tied to a floor anchor; played solo or in pairs.
Two-player paddle game played on water with a rubber ball.
Two-handed racket game: a small racket worn over each hand's knuckles to punch a ball off walls, solo or racquetball-style against an opponent.
Tennis played on a pickleball-size court with a regular tennis racket and a special ball, under USTA tennis rules with small-court changes.
Social team game that grew out of tennis; there is no serving, so it is easier to start than tennis.
Table-size version of pickleball, played on a 9 x 5 ft table with a paddle and a plastic ball.
Small-court, tennis-style game played with box-shaped wooden bats called thugs and tennis balls, scored like tennis. Devised in the 1930s for clubs short on space.
Racquetball played outdoors against one or three walls; there is no standard court size, and World Outdoor Racquetball play allows a single serve only.
Table game that combines padel and ping pong, played with paddles.
Hybrid of tennis and table tennis; the name echoes the sound of the ball.
Badminton-style game played with a hard pickleball paddle and a shuttlecock over a net on a 44 x 20 ft indoor court. First recorded at a US middle school.
Beach Tennis with volleyball-style scoring and a volleyball-height net.
Racket sport where both players stand on one side of the net and hit a ball tethered to a cord.
Four-a-side game using tennis rackets and a hollow see-through ball to score in hockey-size goals. Created in Missouri in 2016.
Indoor wall game between squash and racquetball, played with a racket and a rubber ball. It can be played on any public squash court.
Pickleball played on sand, similar to beach pickleball, on a 44 x 20 ft court.
School racket game with paddles and a shuttlecock, played cooperatively or competitively, with or without a net.
Fast racket sport on a pickleball-size court, played with string rackets and a high-bounce foam ball.
Team game from Switzerland for school PE: players pass a foam ball with small rackets and score in 2 m wide goals. Played in gyms or outdoors; walls count as part of the court.
Tennis played with a soft, hollow rubber ball; popular in Japan and across Asia.
Solo game similar to tether tennis, played with a paddle and a ball.
Swiss school racket game: three squares drawn on the ground with the middle one unplayed; the ball bounces once before each return and smashing downward is not allowed.
Street game derived from road tennis, played on a small 21 x 10 ft court with a racket and a felt rubber ball.
Solo skill game: keep a rubber ball tied to a small paddle by an elastic string bouncing for as many hits in a row as you can.
Squash played on a ping pong table leaned against a wall, hitting the ball off the table and the wall, so it can be played anywhere there is a table.
Chinese net game, also called Roliball: players catch and swing a sand-filled rubber ball with a silicone-membrane racket over a net. Singles or doubles. Began in 1991 in Shanxi.
Argentine tennis variant played with a wooden paddle instead of a strung racket, on a smaller court. Born in Santa Fe in the 1940s.
Team game that mixes tennis and baseball, played on grass with a racket and a felt rubber ball.
Tennis played in threes on a full 78 x 36 ft court, for six to eight players.
Team field game, also called tennis polo: pass and carry a tennis ball and score by throwing it past a goalkeeper who defends with a racket.
Two players hit a ball tied to a pole with rackets or paddles, trying to wind the rope round the pole in their own direction (sold as Swingball).
Compact version of tennis with foam balls and short rackets on a small court.
Racket game played inside a circle around a central post: players hit the ball over the post and within the circle. No net, no halves; singles or doubles.
Racquetball played with a soft foam ball on a 40 x 20 ft indoor court.
Racquetball meets table tennis: two players stand along a ping pong table set 14 inches from a wall and hit the ball across the net and off the wall.
Racket game with no net: players hit a speeder shuttle between two ground zones, mostly outdoors.
Doubles paddle game on a raised, screened-in outdoor platform popular in cold climates; the screens are in play.
A smaller-court version of tennis (also called paddle tennis) played with solid paddles on an open concrete court with a low net and no walls. Not padel, which is played on a walled glass court.
Paddle game for two on the curved Teq table, the same table used for Teqpong; run by FITEQ.
Table-tennis-style paddle game for two on the curved Teq table, the same table used for Teqis; run by FITEQ.
Racket game on a pickleball-size court with a quiet foam ball; there is no non-volley zone and a ball that clips the net stays in play.
